comparator.sourceNotes: The normalized target is the generic 180-EC European Languages and Cultures bachelor. The current official curriculum requires one major language and specialization in one or two of three profiles from Year 2. No profile or major language is substantively more representative of the generic degree. The European Language and Society profile and German major are therefore instantiated through the official-order tie-break: Language and Society is listed first among the profiles, and German is listed first among the major-language options. The pathway preserves the formal 60-EC structure of each year, the 10-EC restricted elective, the 30-EC minor, the 10-EC thesis and every language-specific component without inventing optional content.

routeSelection.route: German major language — European Language and Society profile
routeSelection.basis: The generic programme offers eight major languages and three formal profiles. Current official evidence does not establish one as more representative or more general, so the first-listed profile and first-listed language are selected neutrally, without reference to UCR fit.

exception.reason: The Groningen programme is defined by cumulative proficiency in a chosen European language and by language-specific study through that language. The neutral pathway contains 30 EC of staged German proficiency, 15 EC of German language-specific work across language and society, culture and literature, and politics and society, a further 10-EC interdisciplinary German module, and a thesis grounded in the selected language and profile. UCR's current catalogue contains no German course and no sustained sequence in any European language comparable to this requirement. Its single introductory Dutch course does not create a major-language pathway. UCR literature, media, history, politics, sociology and communication courses can support comparative European questions, but they cannot supply the language competence on which the defining profile and language-specific modules depend. A 24-course response would therefore be a broad European humanities and social-science programme without the programme's central language curriculum, not a defensible closest match.
exception.curriculumContext: The current official curriculum totals exactly 180 EC: a 60-EC first year combining two major-language modules with introductions to all three profiles, academic skills and a faculty-wide course; a 60-EC second year containing the third proficiency module, profile study, a restricted elective, three language-specific modules and a faculty-wide course; and a 60-EC third year containing a 30-EC minor, an interdisciplinary language-specific module, two profile courses and a 10-EC thesis. The German major and European Language and Society profile follow the neutral official-order tie-break; the restricted elective and minor remain open rather than being filled with invented content.
exception.ucrCourseEvidence: Reviewed all 151 current enriched UCR course rows with course descriptions, outline-derived profiles, disciplines, topics, methods, prerequisites and Fall-2026 cohort scheduling. MCCCOMM112 Dutch is the only course whose primary purpose is proficiency in a European language; it is one introductory 7.5-EC course and does not continue into intermediate or advanced study. UCR offers no German course and no sequence in French, Italian, Russian, Spanish or Swedish. MCCCOMM211 Style & Meaning and HCBCOGN312 Psycholinguistics support general linguistic analysis; MCCLITR courses support literature; MCCMEDI courses support media and cultural analysis; and GOSHIST, GOSPOLI, GOSSOCI and GOSLAWJ courses support European historical, political and social study. These courses could form coherent European Studies or communication programmes, but they cannot reproduce cumulative major-language proficiency, language-specific profile study and a thesis grounded in that language. Because the missing language sequence is the degree's academic foundation rather than a peripheral specialty, 23 non-PPD UCR courses cannot form a defensible European Languages and Cultures programme.
